title: Integrating Natural Light for Wellbeing, Performance, and Quality Care Delivery in Healthcare Environments
research_question:
1. What is the relationship between the current lighting conditions in healthcare environments and personnel wellbeing, considering circadian rhythm, mood, alertness, and subjective performance?
2. What is the correlation between healthcare personnel's subjective perceptions of illuminance levels and objective measurements, and how do these findings align with established standards for workstation activities?
3. What are the preferences of healthcare professionals regarding the use of natural light, and how do they perceive its impact on wellbeing and job performance?
4. What are the potential implications of these preferences for the design of healthcare facilities?

participants.description: Healthcare workers (doctors, nurses, midwives, pharmacists, physiotherapists) in a hospital in Abuja, Nigeria. Quantitative survey: 78.2% female, 21.8% male. Age groups: 18-29 (43.6%), 30-39 (40.2%), 40-49 (15.6%), 50-59 (0.7%). Qualitative interviews: 16 participants (10 female, 6 male) from surgical, postnatal, paediatrics, GOPD, and obstetrics departments, aged 18-49.
participants.recruitment: Purposive sampling for quantitative survey (108 participants, 450 responses) and qualitative interviews (16 participants) based on specific criteria and availability.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Indoor lighting conditions (light source, illuminance levels, use of daylight, glare, unwanted shadows) in five hospital wards (surgical, post-natal, paediatrics, obstetrics, General Outpatient Department - GOPD) at Federal Medical Centre, Jabi, Abuja, Nigeria. Workstations were categorized by proximity to windows (next to, away with view, far without view).

measures.instrument: HOBO MX2202 Temp/Light data logger sensors, handheld digital lux meter

measures.construct: Perception of lighting conditions (light source, light levels, use of daylight, glare, unwanted shadow)

findings.antecedent: Lighting characteristics (light sources, light levels, use of daylight)
findings.mechanism: Participants' perceptions of lighting characteristics were relatively consistent across the board, indicating general dissatisfaction.
findings.quote: Around seventy percent of the participants expressed dissatisfaction with at least one of the three lighting characteristics, including light sources, light levels, and use of daylight.

findings.mechanism: Daylight use received the lowest satisfaction rating among lighting characteristics.
findings.quote: lowest rating recorded for the use of daylight at a score of 2.33.

findings.mechanism: Unwanted shadows were perceived as a significant source of disturbance.
findings.quote: highest average score among the two lighting disturbances was observed for the unwanted shadow condition, with a score of 3.16

findings.mechanism: A significant majority of respondents believed lighting conditions adversely affected their task performance.
findings.quote: 75.3% of respondents believed that lighting had an adverse effect on their task performance

findings.mechanism: Over half of the respondents reported adverse effects on wellbeing due to lighting conditions, with eyestrain being the most common complaint.
findings.quote: over half of the respondents (52%) reported adverse effects of lighting conditions on their wellbeing, with eye strain being the most common complaint (33%).

findings.consequent: Preference for brighter lighting at workstations
findings.mechanism: A significant majority of personnel expressed a desire for brighter lighting conditions.
findings.quote: most respondents (87.3%) indicated a preference for brighter lighting conditions at their workstations

findings.consequent: Negative effects of glare on driving performance (GOPD)
findings.mechanism: Older individuals (40+) are more sensitive to glare, experiencing more pronounced negative effects.
findings.quote: significant differences in the effect of glare between ages 18-29 and ages 40 and above (M.W = 35, Z = -2.981, Sig = 0.026)

findings.consequent: Negative effects of glare on surgical performance (Surgical ward)
findings.mechanism: Older individuals (40+) are more sensitive to glare, experiencing more pronounced negative effects.
findings.quote: significant differences in the effect of glare between ages 18-29 and ages 40 and above (M.W = 441, Z = -2.563, Sig = 0.010)

findings.consequent: Negative effects of glare on surgical performance (Surgical ward)
findings.mechanism: Older individuals (40+) are more sensitive to glare, experiencing more pronounced negative effects.
findings.quote: between ages 30-39 and ages 40 and above (M.W = 266.0, Z = -2.369, Sig = 0.018).

findings.consequent: Perception of glare effect in surgical ward
findings.mechanism: Nurses perceive the effect of glare more than doctors in the surgical ward.
findings.quote: The Mann-Whitney U test shows a significant difference (p<0.05) between nurses and doctors regarding the effect of glare.

findings.consequent: Preferred light levels in surgical ward
findings.mechanism: Doctors prefer higher light levels in the surgical ward than nurses.
findings.quote: The Mann-Whitney U test shows a significant difference (p<0.05) between doctors and nurses regarding the light level.

findings.consequent: Perception of glare effect in surgical ward
findings.mechanism: No significant difference in glare perception between midwives and nurses.
findings.quote: the Mann-Whitney U test shows no significant difference (p>0.05) between nurses and midwives regarding the effect of glare.

findings.mechanism: No significant difference in preferred light levels between midwives and nurses.
findings.quote: the Mann-Whitney U test shows no significant difference (p>0.05) between nurses and midwives regarding the light level.

findings.consequent: Perception of glare effect in surgical ward
findings.mechanism: No significant difference in glare perception between doctors and midwives.
findings.quote: the Mann-Whitney U test shows no significant difference (p>0.05) between doctors and midwives regarding the effect of glare.

findings.mechanism: No significant difference in preferred light levels between doctors and midwives.
findings.quote: the Mann-Whitney U test shows no significant difference (p>0.05) between doctors and midwives regarding the light level.

findings.antecedent: Lighting conditions (glare, shadow, satisfaction with light levels)
findings.consequent: Personnel wellbeing (health impacts vs. no health impacts) in GOPD
findings.mechanism: No significant differences were observed in the impact of lighting conditions on wellbeing in the GOPD department based on reported health impacts.
findings.quote: no significant differences were observed in the impact of glare, shadow, or satisfaction with light levels on wellbeing between individuals reporting health impacts and those not reporting such impacts.

findings.consequent: Personnel wellbeing (health impacts vs. no health impacts) in Obstetrics department
findings.mechanism: Individuals reporting health impacts indicated a more negative impact of shadows.
findings.quote: those reporting health impacts indicated a more negative impact of shadows.

findings.consequent: Personnel wellbeing (health impacts vs. no health impacts) in Paediatric department
findings.mechanism: Individuals reporting health impacts experienced more adverse effects of both glare and shadow on their wellbeing.
findings.quote: individuals reporting health impacts experienced more adverse effects of both glare and shadow on their wellbeing compared to counterparts without such impacts.

findings.consequent: Personnel wellbeing (health impacts vs. no health impacts) in Post-Natal department
findings.mechanism: Individuals reporting health impacts indicated a more negative glare impact on wellbeing.
findings.quote: individuals reporting health impacts indicated a more negative glare impact on wellbeing.

findings.consequent: Personnel wellbeing (health impacts vs. no health impacts) in Surgical department
findings.mechanism: Individuals reporting health impacts experienced more adverse effects of both glare and shadow on their wellbeing, alongside lower satisfaction with light levels.
findings.quote: individuals reporting health impacts experienced more adverse effects of both glare and shadow on their wellbeing, alongside lower satisfaction with light levels.

findings.mechanism: Significant differences in perceived light level were observed across various activities, with personal time having the highest mean rank.
findings.quote: significant difference observed across various activities (χ2 = 42.552, p < .001), with the mean rank for personal time being the highest (354.53).

findings.mechanism: Significant differences in satisfaction with light level were observed across activities, with therapy having the highest mean rank.
findings.quote: significant difference across different activities (χ2 = 23.557, p < .001), with therapy having the highest mean rank (344.50)

findings.mechanism: Significant differences in preference for light level were observed across activities, with pre-examination having the highest mean rank.
findings.quote: The preference for light level also showed a significant difference across different activities (χ2 = 30.190, p < .001), with the mean rank for pre-examination being the highest (327.05)

findings.consequent: Effect of lighting conditions on performance
findings.mechanism: No significant difference was found in the effect of lighting conditions on performance across different activities.
findings.quote: no significant difference in the effect of lighting conditions on performance across different activities (χ2 = 7.398, p = .389).

findings.mechanism: Nurses reported significantly higher satisfaction with light levels compared to midwives.
findings.quote: the mean rank for nurses was significantly higher than that for midwives (185.20 vs. 155.06, sig = 0.001).

findings.mechanism: Doctors reported significantly higher satisfaction with light level compared to midwives.
findings.quote: for doctors and midwives, the mean rank for doctors was significantly higher than that for midwives (158.37 vs. 113.94, Z = -4.254, sig = 0.000).

findings.mechanism: Nurses showed a significantly lower preference for light level compared to doctors.
findings.quote: the mean rank for nurses was lower than that for doctors (211.53 vs. 190.09), and the difference was statistically significant (sig = 0.034).

findings.mechanism: Doctors showed a significantly lower preference for light level compared to midwives.
findings.quote: for doctors and midwives, the mean rank for doctors was lower than that for Midwives, and the difference was statistically significant (144.95 vs. 117.14, sig = 0.005).

findings.mechanism: The light level was significantly higher for doctors than midwives.
findings.quote: for doctors and midwives, the mean rank for doctors was significantly higher than that for midwives (147.87 vs. 116.45, sig = 0.002).

findings.consequent: Preference for light level and satisfaction with light level
findings.mechanism: The pre-examination activity category consistently showed the highest preference and satisfaction with light level across all pairwise comparisons.
findings.quote: The Pre-examination category consistently showed a significantly higher preference of light and satisfaction with light level compared to the other categories.

findings.consequent: Negative impact on health (eyestrain, headaches) and job performance (difficulty concentrating, interpreting prescriptions, occupational hazards)
findings.mechanism: Healthcare professionals reported that inadequate illumination leads to visual strain, reduced focus, discomfort, and potential occupational hazards.
findings.quote: 68.75% of those interviewed indicated that the lighting levels in their workplaces were insufficient...

findings.mechanism: A majority of healthcare professionals exclusively preferred natural light over artificial light or a combination.
findings.quote: the majority (62.5%) exclusively preferred natural light.

findings.consequent: Improved mood, reduced stress, enhanced cognitive function, increased alertness, vitamin D production, patient recovery, staff morale, productivity
findings.mechanism: Natural light is perceived as a key factor in fostering a healing environment, boosting staff morale, and enhancing productivity due to its various positive effects.
findings.quote: Natural light is identified as a key factor in fostering a healing environment, boosting staff morale, and enhancing productivity.

findings.antecedent: Building obstructions (nearby buildings, frosted glass, obstructive vegetation)
findings.mechanism: Physical barriers in the built environment directly block the entry of natural light into workspaces.
findings.quote: The physical environment surrounding the workspace also plays a pivotal role, with factors like frosted glass, nearby buildings, or obstructive vegetation negatively impacting the experience...

findings.consequent: Eyestrain, headaches, mood fluctuations, reduced focus
findings.mechanism: Personnel reported experiencing negative wellbeing symptoms during overcast weather when inadequate lighting was more pronounced.
findings.quote: personnel reported experiencing eyestrain and mood fluctuations during overcast weather when inadequate lighting was more pronounced.

findings.mechanism: Females exhibited greater sensitivity and more pronounced negative effects from low light levels across various hospital wards.
findings.quote: This gender disparity was confirmed through post hoc Mann-Whitney tests, which revealed a more pronounced effect of light level on females across various hospital wards.

findings.consequent: Perception of room light as less bright and inappropriate
findings.mechanism: Age-related visual impairments may lead older participants to perceive room light as less bright and inappropriate.
findings.quote: older participants consistently perceiving room light as less bright and inappropriate compared to their younger counterparts.

findings.consequent: Perception of glare and shadow as more problematic (GOPD ward)
findings.mechanism: Shorter working hours were associated with higher mean ranks for glare and shadow effects, indicating these were perceived as more problematic.
findings.quote: working hours of less than 6 hours were associated with higher mean ranks for the effects of glare and shadow, indicating that these lighting conditions were perceived to be more problematic during shorter working hours (SIG=0.004).

findings.consequent: Perception of shadow as more problematic (Obstetrics ward)
findings.mechanism: Longer working hours were associated with a higher mean rank for the effect of shadow, indicating it was perceived as more problematic.
findings.quote: a higher mean rank for the effect of shadow was observed during longer working hours, indicating that this lighting condition was perceived to be more problematic during longer working hours.

findings.mechanism: Satisfaction with lighting was higher during shorter working hours.
findings.quote: a higher mean rank for satisfaction with light level was observed during shorter working hours, indicating that satisfaction with lighting was higher during shorter working hours.

findings.mechanism: Satisfaction with lighting was higher during longer working hours.
findings.quote: a higher mean rank for satisfaction with light level was observed during longer working hours, indicating that satisfaction with lighting was higher during longer working hours.

mechanisms: Inadequate lighting leads to reduced satisfaction and morale, increased errors, increased stress and burnout, disrupted circadian rhythms, impaired sleep patterns, physical discomfort (eyestrain, headaches), reduced focus, compromised visibility, and occupational hazards.

Adequate natural light improves mood, reduces stress, enhances cognitive function, increases alertness, supports vitamin D production, leads to better sleep patterns, faster patient recovery, increased job satisfaction, improved productivity, energy savings, reliability during power outages, and provides inspiration and uplifting feelings.
Age-related visual impairments influence the perception of light levels.
Gender differences affect sensitivity to low light levels and concerns about lighting impact.
Job-specific demands and responsibilities influence lighting preferences and satisfaction.
Environmental factors like weather conditions and building obstructions directly impact natural light availability and its perceived effects.
implementation_implications: Prioritize user-centred design in healthcare facilities to meet diverse needs.
Integrate natural light into architectural designs by optimizing window placement, ward layout, building orientation, and incorporating green spaces.
Enhance artificial lighting systems through brightness optimization, stability, and adaptability.
Develop new criteria for lighting standards and revise existing guidelines to prioritize occupant wellbeing and performance.
Implement emergency lighting systems to ensure safety and functionality during power failures.
Adopt a participatory design approach, involving healthcare personnel in the design process to ensure their preferences and needs are met.

limitations: Unforeseen impact of external events (COVID-19 pandemic) led to reduced investigation period and limited geographic diversity, hindering observation of seasonal daylight variations.
Exclusion of individual behavioural characteristics (personal preferences, psychological aspects) due to complexity and variability, potentially leading to an incomplete understanding.
Reliance on subjective assessments for performance measurement, susceptible to response biases and inaccuracies.
Limited generalisability of findings to healthcare environments in other climatic regions due to study's focus on Abuja, Nigeria.

Isolation of indoor lighting conditions without explicit consideration of interactions with other environmental factors (noise, air quality, temperature), potentially leading to an incomplete understanding of overall environmental impact.
